passages.text: Our father said, ‘You seem to me to be saying many reasonable things.’ Peter said, ‘Tell me, then, what is holding you back from coming to our faith, so that we may begin to speak directly to it. There are many things that hold people back. For those already convinced, there are the demands of purchases, business, farming, anxieties, and things of that sort. For unbelievers, among whom you too belong, there are assumptions: thinking that gods who do not exist do exist, or that everything is subject to birth-fate or to chance, or that souls are mortal, or that our message is false because there is no providence.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: everything is subject to birth-fate
lexical_decisions.rationale: Genesis here can denote the determining configuration or fate associated with birth, as distinguished from chance in the next alternative. Birth-fate keeps the birth wording visible; fate determined by the stars at birth is a fuller contextual alternative, but stars are not expressly named in this clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: chance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun refers to spontaneous occurrence without directing providence. It is not rendered automation, a misleading modern technical association.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the demands of purchases, business, farming, anxieties
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural occupations or lack of leisure is the governing idea, and all four listed sources of preoccupation are retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ θεοὺς τοὺς οὐκ ὄντας εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: thinking that gods who do not exist do exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes the substantivized not-being expression existentially, so that the error concerns treating nonexistent gods as existent. This follows the explicit being/not-being contrast in the phrase. A material predicative alternative is thinking that those who are not gods are gods, which denies their divinity rather than their existence. The main text does not claim that the existential attachment is unique.

passages.text: ‘But I say that everything is governed by God's providence, judging from what has happened to you: your separation from your family for so many years. Since, if they had remained with you, perhaps they would not have listened to the teachings of reverence for God, their journey abroad with their mother was arranged, along with shipwreck, presumed death, and loss of contact. So too was their education in Greek and godless doctrines, so that, knowing them, they might be better able to refute them. After this came their love for the teaching of reverence for God and their ability to join me in helping my proclamation; then their brother Clement's coming together with us, and thus their mother's being recognized and becoming fully convinced of the divinity through healing. Shortly afterward came the twins' being recognized and recognizing in turn, and, on the following day, meeting you and your recovering your family. I do not think that so great and swift a harmony, converging from every direction upon one intended aim, is without providence.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ναυφραγίῳ καὶ θανάτου ὑπονοίᾳ καὶ ἀπαρτίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: along with shipwreck, presumed death, and loss of contact
lexical_decisions.rationale: The list describes the circumstances of the family separation. Ἀπαρτία is read as absence of news or contact in this context; the translation does not supply a particular duration beyond the previously stated years.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὕτως τὴν μητέρα ἐπιγνωσθῆναι καὶ ὑπὸ θεραπείας τὴν θεότητα πληροφορηθῆναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: and thus their mother's being recognized and becoming fully convinced of the divinity through healing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text continues the mother as the inferred subject of the second passive infinitive and takes the accusative divinity as the content of her conviction. That connects her recognition with her resulting assurance. A material alternative takes divinity as the expressed accusative subject of that infinitive, parallel to mother as subject of the first: and the divinity was fully confirmed through healing. Neither reading establishes whose divinity is meant, and the English does not identify Peter or the mother as divine.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ δίδυμα τέκνα ἐπιγνωσθέντα καὶ ἐπιγνόντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the twins' being recognized and recognizing in turn
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both passive and active recognition are retained. The unexpressed object of their recognition is not replaced by an invented named person in this clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: upon one intended aim
lexical_decisions.rationale: The convergence is toward one aim of intention or purpose. Agreement of belief is a possible contextual emphasis for γνώμη, but the preceding arrangement of events favors an intended aim without naming a separate planner in this phrase.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so great and swift a harmony
lexical_decisions.rationale: The degree of magnitude expressed by τοσαύτην is distinguished from the speed expressed by ταχεῖαν, rather than collapsing both into so swift.

passages.text: Our father began to say to Peter, ‘Do not suppose, my dearest Peter, that I have not been thinking about the message you proclaim. Indeed, at the end of this past night, when Clement urged me at length to agree with the truth you proclaim, I answered, “What newer instruction can anyone give beyond what the ancients advised?” He smiled gently and said, “There is a great difference, father, between the teachings of reverence for God and those of philosophy. For the message of truth has its proof from prophecy, whereas the teaching of philosophy offers fine language and seems to present its proofs from conjectures.” Having said this, however, he set out for me, as an example, the teaching about love for humanity that you had explained to him. It seemed to me, rather, utterly unjust. I will tell you how. He said that it was just for someone to offer the other cheek as well to the person striking his cheek; to give his head-covering too to the person taking his cloak; to go two miles with the person compelling him to go one; and other things of this sort.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καλλιλογίας παρέχων ἐκ στοχασμῶν δοκεῖ παριστᾶν τὰς ἀποδείξεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the teaching of philosophy offers fine language and seems to present its proofs from conjectures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The favorable-sounding language and the qualification seems are retained alongside the criticism of conjectural proofs. The translation does not replace conjecture by observation or prophecy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν περὶ φιλανθρωπίας μοι ἐξέθετο λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he set out for me ... the teaching about love for humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term is a broad humane love or kindness toward human beings. Love for humanity keeps its human object explicit and connects it with the ensuing discussion of humane treatment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his head-covering
lexical_decisions.rationale: The garment can be a scarf, kerchief, or head-covering. It is distinguished from the cloak named immediately before it, rather than replaced by the tunic familiar from another form of the saying.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Having said this, however
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verified selected print reads ὁμῶς, not the usual adversative accentuation ὅμως. The main text interprets the continuation adversatively: after contrasting the two teachings he nevertheless gives the example. Non-adversative alike or together is a lexical alternative for the printed form. This interpretation is not a change to the source or a claim that the Greek has been normalized to ὅμως.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘But you judged unjust what is most just. If you wish, listen.’ The father said, ‘I very much wish to.’ Peter said, ‘Suppose there are two hostile kings, each with a separate territory. If one king's subject is discovered in the other's country and thereby owes death, but is released from punishment with a slap rather than death, does not the one who released him appear humane?’ The father said, ‘Very much so.’ Peter said, ‘What, then, if this same man takes from someone something of that person's own, or even something belonging to someone else, and is caught for it? If he gives double, although he owes fourfold and death because he was caught within the enemy's borders, does it not seem to you that the one who took double and released him from death is humane?’ The father said, ‘It appears so.’ Peter said, ‘What then? Should not someone in another's kingdom, and that of a wicked enemy at that, for the sake of staying alive, flatter everyone, yield beyond what is demanded by those who compel service, greet those who do not greet him, reconcile enemies, avoid quarreling with angry people, freely provide his possessions to everyone who asks, and do other things of this sort?’ The father said, ‘I would all the more reasonably endure everything, if indeed he puts staying alive before these things.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἴδιόν τι τινὸς αὐτὸς οὗτος ἀφέληται ἢ καὶ ἀλλότριον
lexical_decisions.chosen: this same man takes from someone something of that person's own, or even something belonging to someone else
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is read as the victim's own property versus another person's property in the victim's possession. An alternative takes own in relation to the person doing the taking. The main rendering makes the contextual property relations intelligible without changing the two expressed categories into a single generic theft.

lexical_decisions.chosen: yield beyond what is demanded by those who compel service
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb refers to impressed or compulsory service, with yielding to a greater extent. The rendering retains the excess compliance without introducing a specific journey or distance into this general instruction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ἀδεῶς παντὶ αἰτοῦντι παρέχειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: freely provide his possessions to everyone who asks
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἀδεῶς can mean without fear or hesitation. Freely is read as unhesitating willingness, not a claim that the hostile country is safe or that the possessions carry no monetary value.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if indeed he puts staying alive before these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source moves from the father's first-person willingness to an expressed third-person verb. He retains the hypothetical person as its subject rather than silently replacing it with I; the comparison is preference for life over the burdens just listed.

passages.text: Peter said, ‘Is it not, then, the case that those whom you said were being wronged are themselves trespassers, since they are in another's kingdom, and are taking more than their due to the extent that they possess anything? Those thought to be doing wrong grant each person on the opposing side as much as they allow that person to have. For these things belong to those who have chosen the present. They are so humane as even to permit them to live. That is how the illustration stands; now hear the actual matter. When the prophet of truth was present, he taught us that the creator and God of all assigned two kingdoms to two beings, a good one and an evil one. He gave the evil one the kingdom of this present world, together with a law, so that he might have authority to punish wrongdoers; to the good one, the coming eternal age. He made each human being free, with authority to assign himself to whichever he wishes: either the present evil or the future good. Those who have chosen the present have authority to be rich, live luxuriously, enjoy themselves, and do whatever they can, for they will have none of the good things to come. But those who have decided to receive the things of the future kingdom may not consider any of the things here their own, since they belong to another king, except only water and bread—and these obtained with sweat to sustain life, since voluntary death is not permitted—and also a single covering. For one is not allowed to stand naked because of heaven, which sees everything.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτοὶ παρορισταὶ τυγχάνουσιν, καθὰ ἐν ἑτέρου εἰσὶν βασιλείᾳ, καὶ τοσοῦτον πλεονέκται εἰσίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: trespassers ... taking more than their due
lexical_decisions.rationale: These words occur in the clause about being in another's kingdom. The first denotes crossing a boundary, the second grasping or claiming an excessive share. The rendering does not replace their property-based accusation by a general description of sinful attitudes.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δυσίν τισιν ἀπένειμεν· βασιλείας δύο, ἀγαθῷ τε καὶ πονηρῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: assigned two kingdoms to two beings, a good one and an evil one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two recipients are distinct from the creator assigning their realms. The English supplies beings for the substantivized adjectives without naming either as a second creator or as a particular named angel.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ τῷ παρόντι κακῷ ἢ τῷ μέλλοντι ἀγαθῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: either the present evil or the future good
lexical_decisions.rationale: These substantivized adjective forms permit reference to the present evil and future good as conditions or realms, alongside the preceding recipients of the kingdoms. The translation retains the broad evil/good antithesis instead of forcing every occurrence to name an individual being; the inflected forms themselves do not settle masculine versus neuter reference.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of heaven, which sees everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: Heaven is the expressed all-seeing subject. It may function as a reverential reference to heavenly observation, but the main text does not silently replace it with God or infer a particular observer.

passages.text: ‘If, then, you wish to hear the precise account of the matter, those whom you said a little earlier were being wronged are, rather, themselves doing wrong. For they, having chosen what is to come, live in the present among the wicked, sharing many of the same things with them: life itself, light, bread, water, clothing, and some other things of that kind. But those whom you thought were doing wrong share nothing with the good men in the things to come.’ The father answered, ‘Now that you have persuaded me that those doing wrong are themselves being wronged, while those being wronged are instead taking more than their due, the whole matter seems to me even more utterly unjust. Those who seem to be doing wrong permit many things to those who chose the future; those who seem to be wronged themselves do wrong, because there they do not provide equivalent things to those who permitted them here what they themselves permitted them.’ Peter said, ‘This is not unjust either, because each person has authority to choose the present or the future, whether small or great. A person who has chosen by his own judgment and will is not wronged—not even, I say, if he chooses the small things, since the great things lay before him; for the small things too lay before him.’ The father said, ‘You have spoken rightly. For one of the Greek sages has also said, “Responsibility belongs to those who choose; God is not responsible.”’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ δὲ ἀδικεῖν ὑπὸ σοῦ νομισθέντες ἐν τοῖς ἐσομένοις ἀγαθοῖς ἀνδράσιν οὐδὲν συνυπάρχουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: those whom you thought were doing wrong share nothing with the good men in the things to come
lexical_decisions.rationale: Good men is read together as the persons with whom no future sharing occurs. A possible alternative takes good with future good things; the supplied masculine ἀγαθοῖς ἀνδράσιν supports the main attachment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what they themselves permitted them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated pronouns return to the present-world benefactors and the recipients. The English retains the repetition of granting rather than adding a new category of compensation absent from the clause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ προέκειτο τὰ μεγάλα· προέκειτο γὰρ αὐτῷ καὶ τὰ μικρά
lexical_decisions.chosen: since the great things lay before him; for the small things too lay before him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both statements about available choices, in their printed order, are retained. The repetition is not silently rewritten into a different conditional argument.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Responsibility belongs to those who choose; God is not responsible
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast concerns accountability or blame for choice. The Greek sage remains unnamed because this passage does not identify him.

passages.text: ‘But explain this argument to me as well. I remember Clement telling me that we suffer wrongs and sufferings for the forgiveness of sins.’ Peter said, ‘That too is right. For we who have chosen the future, when we possess things in excess—whether clothes, food, drink, or anything else—possess sins, because we ought to have nothing, as I explained a little earlier. For all, possessions are sins. Their deprivation, however it happens, is a removal of sins.’ The father said, ‘It follows, as you have distinguished two territories of the two kings, leaving each of those under their authority to choose what he wishes. But what about sufferings? Do we suffer these justly too?’ Peter said, ‘Most justly. Since the rule for those being saved is, as I said, that no one should possess anything, yet many possess many things—which are, in other words, sins—for this reason, out of God's surpassing love for humanity, sufferings are brought upon those who do not live with complete sincerity. This is so that, because of their measure of love for God, they may be saved from eternal punishments through temporary penalties.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: For all, possessions are sins
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative all and the wordplay between possessions and sins are retained as Peter's claim within this argument. The categorical wording is not softened into merely a warning against excessive attachment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the rule for those being saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ὅρος can mean a boundary, definition, or determining rule. Here the following infinitive gives a rule of possession; territorial boundary remains a live echo of the preceding kingdoms illustration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who do not live with complete sincerity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb concerns purity or sincerity of conduct. Completely is not an invented moral intensifier but expresses the adverb's undiluted quality; live purely is a concise alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὸ ποσῶς φιλόθεον προσκαίροις τιμωρίαις αἰωνίων σωθῶσιν κολάσεων
lexical_decisions.chosen: because of their measure of love for God, they may be saved from eternal punishments through temporary penalties
lexical_decisions.rationale: The limited degree of God-love is retained, as is the contrast between temporary and eternal punishment. The translation does not add a named intermediate place or impose a later doctrinal account of the mechanism.

passages.text: The father said, ‘What then? Do we not see many impious people who are poor? Are these too among those being saved just because of that?’ Peter said, ‘Not necessarily. Poverty is not acceptable if someone desires what he ought not. Thus some are rich in their intention while poor in money, and are punished as people desiring to grasp more than their due. Nor is someone necessarily righteous simply because he is poor. He may be destitute in money yet desire or even do what he ought above all not to do. He may worship idols, blaspheme, engage in sexual immorality, or live indifferently, whether swearing falsely, lying, or living unfaithfully. Nevertheless, our teacher pronounced the faithful poor blessed—not because they had provided anything, for they had nothing, but because, committing no sin, they cannot be condemned solely for not giving alms because they have nothing.’ The father said, ‘Truly, the facts seem entirely consistent with the premise. That is why I have decided to hear the whole account in order.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: are rich in their intention while poor in money
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is between chosen desire and actual means, not a claim that the poor secretly possess wealth. Intention preserves the volitional force of προαίρεσις.

lexical_decisions.chosen: live indifferently
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this list of wrongdoing, indifference concerns disregard for moral distinctions rather than an absence of strong emotion. The following oath-breaking, lying, and unfaithfulness illustrate the conduct.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μηδὲν ἁμαρτάνοντες, ἐπὶ μόνῳ τῷ τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην μὴ ποιεῖν διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν καταδικασθῆναι οὐκ ἔχουσι
lexical_decisions.chosen: committing no sin, they cannot be condemned solely for not giving alms because they have nothing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participial qualification is retained; the argument concerns the faithful poor who do not otherwise sin, not a declaration that every poor person is sinless. The two negatives concern not giving and inability to condemn on that sole ground, and are both represented.
